lessons.title: Costs, GST and Tax: How the Two Are Treated Differently

children.text: Neha and Imran each sell a property in Pune in 2026, and each makes a long-term capital gain of exactly ₹1 crore. Neha sold a flat and buys a bigger flat with the money. Her tax bill: nil. Imran sold a shop and wants to buy another shop. His tax bill: ₹12.5 lakh, before surcharge and cess. Same city, same gain, same instinct to reinvest in what they know. Indian tax law treats homes and commercial property very differently, from the day you buy to the day you sell. This lesson walks through those differences so the higher yield on commercial property is judged after tax, not before.

body.text: Indian tax law favours homes. Residential property gets gentler GST treatment and an easy route to tax-free reinvestment. Commercial property pays GST on rent and has no route to reinvest tax-free into another commercial property.

The Income-tax Act, 2025 replaced the 1961 Act from 1 April 2026 and renumbered its sections. This lesson describes provisions by what they do, with the familiar old section names given for reference. Tax rules change often; confirm the current position with a chartered accountant before acting.

children.text: Running costs diverge more than purchase costs. Municipal property tax rates for commercial buildings are usually higher than for homes. Commercial electricity tariffs are higher too, although tenants normally bear them. On the other hand, commercial tenants usually pay common area maintenance, while residential owners often end up paying society maintenance themselves. The biggest holding-period difference is GST on rent.
GST on Rent: The Clearest Dividing Line

columns.label: Residential rent
points: Exempt when a residential dwelling is let for residential use
Exception: if the tenant is GST-registered, it pays 18% GST under reverse charge
Most individual landlords never need GST registration for home rent
No GST invoices or returns for typical family lets

columns.label: Commercial rent
points: Landlord must register once aggregate turnover crosses ₹20 lakh a year (₹10 lakh in special category states)
If the landlord is unregistered and the tenant is registered, the tenant pays GST under reverse charge
Registered landlords must issue invoices and file returns

body.label: GST on commercial rent
body.context: Business tenants usually claim this back as input tax credit, so it rarely reduces your rent. The real cost to you is compliance: registration, invoices, returns and the risk of penalties for mistakes.

markDefs.definition: A GST mechanism where the recipient of a service, rather than the supplier, pays the tax to the government. It applies to certain transactions, such as commercial rent paid by a registered tenant to an unregistered landlord.

children.text: Since October 2024, a GST-registered tenant renting commercial space from an unregistered landlord pays the GST itself under

. That reduces the burden on small landlords below the threshold, but landlords close to it should track their total turnover carefully with a professional, because the definition can include other income.
Income Tax on Rent: Same Head, Same Formula

markDefs.definition: For a let-out property, broadly the annual rent received minus municipal property taxes actually paid by the owner. It is the starting point for taxing rental income.

children.text: Here the two types are treated alike. Rent from both a let-out flat and a let-out shop is taxed as "Income from House Property". You start from the
, take a flat 30% standard deduction for repairs and upkeep, and subtract interest on any loan.

body.caption: The 30% standard deduction applies regardless of actual repair spending. GST collected on rent is not part of rental income.
Tax on one year of rent, 30% slab, no loan, before cess

cells: Rent left after property tax and income tax

children.text: The formula takes a similar bite from both. One difference is the loan. Interest on a let-out property is deductible, but under the old regime any resulting loss can be set off against salary or other income only up to ₹2 lakh a year, with the rest carried forward. Under the new regime, a loss from house property cannot be set off against other income at all. Since residential rent rarely covers loan interest, this limit hits leveraged flat owners hardest.
Tax When You Sell: Where Homes Win Big

Property held for more than 24 months produces a long-term capital gain, taxed at 12.5% without indexation for sales made on or after 23 July 2024. Resident individuals and HUFs selling land or buildings bought before that date can instead choose 20% with indexation if it works out lower. Gains on property held for 24 months or less are taxed at your slab rate. The real difference lies in the exemptions.

body.text: There is no exemption for reinvesting commercial sale proceeds into another commercial property. To avoid tax on selling a shop or office, you must buy a residential house with the entire net sale proceeds, or put up to ₹50 lakh into specified bonds. A flat owner only needs to reinvest the gain itself into another house.

body.title: Tax on a ₹1 crore long-term gain from selling a shop, by route (₹ lakh, before surcharge and cess)

data.label: Buy a house with full net proceeds

body.text: Watch the circle rate. If you sell for more than 10% below the stamp duty value set by the state, the tax department treats the stamp duty value as your sale price for capital gains, and the buyer can also be taxed on the difference. Commercial units in weak markets often trade below circle rates, which makes this a practical trap.

body.title: Calculate: Taxable Rent on a Chennai Shop
body.prompt: You rent a shop in T. Nagar, Chennai for ₹9 lakh a year and pay ₹40,000 in property tax. There is no loan. What is your taxable income from house property, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: Net annual value: ₹9 lakh minus ₹0.4 lakh = ₹8.6 lakh. Standard deduction at 30%: ₹2.58 lakh. Taxable rent: ₹8.6 lakh minus ₹2.58 lakh = ₹6.02 lakh.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: Long-Term Property
body.textWithBlank: Land and buildings become long-term capital assets once held for more than ___ months.
body.explanation: Gains on property held for more than 24 months are long-term, taxed at 12.5% without indexation, with the indexation option still available to resident individuals and HUFs on property bought before 23 July 2024.

body.title: Quick Check: Saving Tax on a Shop Sale
body.question: Imran sells a shop and makes a ₹1 crore long-term gain. Which reinvestment can make the entire gain exempt?
options: Buying another shop with the capital gain
Buying a residential house with the entire net sale proceeds
Buying a pre-leased office within 2 years
body.explanation: For a non-house asset like a shop, full exemption requires investing the entire net sale proceeds in a residential house, subject to conditions. Specified bonds are capped at ₹50 lakh, and there is no exemption for buying another commercial property.

body.title: Scenario: Upgrading a Mumbai Office
body.scenario: Sunil, a resident individual, is selling an office unit in Andheri East for ₹5 crore net of costs. He bought it 12 years ago, and his long-term capital gain is ₹2 crore. He wants to buy a larger pre-leased office in BKC for ₹6 crore. He already owns the flat he lives in and no other house. His CA mentions three options: pay the tax, buy bonds, or buy a residential flat instead.
body.prompt: What does each option mean for Sunil, and how should he decide?
body.modelAnswer: Paying the tax: 12.5% of ₹2 crore is ₹25 lakh before surcharge and cess. He might also compare the 20%-with-indexation option, since he bought before July 2024. Bonds: investing ₹50 lakh in specified bonds within 6 months exempts ₹50 lakh of gain, saving ₹6.25 lakh, but locks the money in low-yield bonds for 5 years. A residential flat: investing the full ₹5 crore net proceeds in a house could exempt the entire gain, since he owns only one other house, but he would give up an 8%-type commercial yield for a 3%-type residential yield. On ₹5 crore, that income gap is roughly ₹25 lakh a year, which erases the ₹25 lakh tax saving within about a year. He should run the after-tax total return of each path rather than chase the exemption. Tax should shape the decision, not dictate it.

points: Purchase costs are broadly similar, though under-construction property carries GST under different rules for homes and commercial units.
Residential rent for residential use is GST-exempt; commercial rent attracts 18% GST, usually passed through to business tenants but adding compliance work.
Rent from both is taxed under house property with a 30% standard deduction, so the income tax bite is similar.
Long-term gains on both are taxed at 12.5% after 24 months, but only homes can be sold and replaced with another home tax-free by reinvesting just the gain.
Selling commercial property tax-free requires buying a residential house with the entire net proceeds, or parking up to ₹50 lakh in specified bonds.
Compare options on after-tax total return; an exemption that pushes you into a much lower-yielding asset can cost more than the tax it saves.
